newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germans feel country is in upheaval - pollster.
newsitem.headline: Germans feel country is in upheaval - pollster.

text.p: Mounting social and economic problems have prompted Germans to lose confidence in a predictable future and see themselves living in a time of upheaval and uncertainty, a leading pollster said on Thursday.

Renate Koecher of the respected Allensbach Institute told a symposium in Bonn that this reaction to heavy job losses and welfare cutbacks was very different to reactions to the country's economic recession four years ago.
Then people saw the recession as just a passing phase.
But now Koecher said there was a feeling of living in times of unpredictability and not being in control, although most people did not see their own financial position getting worse.
"People believe they are living in a time of great upheaval when everyone will have to make big changes."

Germans have been particularly shaken in the last few months by a government austerity programme in which they have seen the welfare benefits they had fought for over decades, and come to see as their birthright, suddenly being cut.

Unemployment has galloped to a post-war record of over 12 percent. This year a government reform commission chipped away at another taboo by telling Germans to expect higher pensions contributions and lower payouts in future.

Koecher said while a growing number of Germans had seen the general need for spending cuts and radical reforms of the welfare system, most did not yet accept that this might mean personal sacrifices or a loss of benefits.

Almost three-quarters of Germans surveyed by Allensbach said they believed the most important achievement of the last term of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's centre-right government had been the introduction of compulsory long-term nursing care insurance -- with attendant increase in social security contributions.

Nevertheless, there were signs that attitudes were changing. Some 40 percent were now prepared to accept the idea of a wage freeze, something that would have been unthinkable in the 1992-1993 recession, she said.
A slim majority of Germans also believed, perhaps for the first time in decades, that they would have to make do with lower pensions as the proportion of old people grew.
Koecher said there was also a growing readiness to make sacrifices on pay if this meant preserving jobs.

But she also noted a dramatic difference in sentiment between west Germany and the formerly communist east, where people had become used to an all-encompassing cradle-to-grave welfare system over decades.
She said east German approval of welfare cuts was practically zero and 61 percent of east Germans thought the current welfare system inadequate.
